paras: In May and June 1903, white men in northern Smith County, Mississippi, near Burns, attacked Black residents after a white farmer named Craft was shot from ambush in a dispute over a Black farmhand who had left a crop. After a second white man, James Boyles, was shot on June 5, four Black men and one Black woman were reported killed, eight or ten beaten and most of the Black community ordered to leave. White papers nationwide called it a “race war,” while the Black press carried only short reprinted items.

According to a Laurel dispatch, a Black man had “pitched” a crop for the Bruce brothers and received a considerable advance on his labor before leaving it. Another version described a family who “tried to jump their crop” and refused Bruce's demand that they return to work or repay the debt.

The Bruces gathered neighbors and went back after the man, and on the way the party was ambushed and Craft was mortally wounded. The white men returned fire and, by the Washington Times version, “killed several of their assailants.” Most versions dated the outbreak to Tuesday, May 12, and all came secondhand from “parties in Laurel,” naming none of the Black dead. Whites were then said to be “scouring the country, shooting and whipping every suspicious negro,” while still hunting the man accused of starting the trouble.

On June 5, news reached Forest that Boyles, a planter, had been shot from ambush by three Black men in the neighborhood where the earlier killing took place. A Forest dispatch of June 8 reported the five killings, the beatings and the expulsion order as the result of the shootings of Craft and Boyles. It attributed them to men from “the noted Sullivan's Hollow community” in southern Smith County, Craft's own section. One report added that two houses were burned.

By June 8 the area was reported quiet, on condition that the Black residents ordered out left “at once.” The names of the dead “could not be learned,” and the men accused of shooting Boyles had not been caught. No report of arrests, an inquest or a prosecution for the killings of Black residents appears in the coverage.

White papers ran the May dispatch under headlines such as “Fierce Race War Occurs Near Burns” and “Bloody Race War Now On in Mississippi.” The St. Paul Globe's headline, “Negroes Ambush Farmers and Pay Dearly for Their Act,” cast the killings as a consequence of the ambush. In June the story ran as “Slaughter of Negroes” in the Washington Times, “Drastic Action by White Avengers” in the Evening Star and “Follows Murder of Two Whites” in the Daily Kennebec Journal, though only one white man had been reported killed.
Closer to the scene, the Hattiesburg Daily Progress described a matching raid in Jones County as a way to “solve the negro problem,” but concluded it was “not a legitimate way.”

The Black press printed only wire items, without comment. The Savannah Tribune condensed the Laurel dispatch on May 23 and on June 13 reported five Black people shot to death “on account of the killing of two white men by two negroes.” The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate reprinted the Forest dispatch as “Kill Five Negroes,” and the Western World printed a garbled Mobile special.

The May dispatches placed the Craft ambush near Burns in Smith County, while the Hattiesburg editorial set apparently the same events in Jones County. Forest dispatches put the Boyles shooting in southern Scott County, but later reports placed it in Smith County. June accounts dated Craft's shooting “last week” or “two weeks ago,” against the May dispatches' May 12. Whether the “several” killed in May are among the five reported in June cannot be determined.

reader.title: Smith County, Mississippi, attacks on Black residents (1903)
bases: Armed whites whipped, shot and killed Black people 'wherever they find them' over several weeks, killing five in one night and ordering most of the community to leave (A1, A2, A27, A29).

Separate dispatches from Laurel in May (A1, A2) and Forest and Memphis in June (A27, A30), plus a Hattiesburg editorial (A10), agree that Craft was shot from ambush and that whites then killed and beat Black residents of northern Smith County.

accounts.label: Laurel wire dispatch (May 15-16)
accounts.gist: A Black man who jumped a crop and his friends threatened the Bruces; the Bruce party was ambushed, Craft mortally wounded, and whites returned fire and began whipping and killing Black people wherever found. The source was 'parties in Laurel' from the neighborhood.

accounts.label: Hattiesburg Daily Progress editorial
accounts.gist: White men passing through a neighborhood of Jones County were fired on and one badly wounded; whites raided every Black house, ran residents out, and 'several' were beaten or shot to death.

accounts.label: Forest dispatch (June 5-9)
accounts.gist: After Boyles was shot from ambush by three Black men, four Black men and a Black woman were killed, eight or ten beaten and most others ordered to leave, by men from Sullivan's Hollow in southern Smith County.

accounts.label: Mobile special to the Globe-Democrat, as printed in a Black weekly
accounts.gist: After an attempt on Boyles late Friday, four Black people including a woman were killed 'last night' and two houses burned, the trouble growing out of the murder of R. O. Craft a few weeks earlier.

framing.detail: Headlines called it a 'Fierce Race War' and 'Bloody Race War' and relayed the whites' account that Black men ambushed first.
The St. Paul Globe headlined 'Negroes Ambush Farmers and Pay Dearly for Their Act.'
The Hattiesburg Daily Progress said Jones County was 'about to solve the negro problem in a new but effective way' but called it 'not a legitimate way.'
June headlines ranged from 'Slaughter of Negroes' and 'Reign of Lawlessness' to 'Drastic Action by White Avengers' and 'Follows Murder of Two Whites.'
The Savannah Tribune, Wisconsin Weekly Advocate and Western World ran short wire items without comment.

conflicts.note: The Laurel and Forest wires agree on northern Smith County; the Hattiesburg editorial gives no names and may be misplacing the same events.
The June 5 Forest dispatches are the earliest and most specific; A28 says it was the same neighborhood as the earlier killing.

Unnamed Black residents: 'several' killed in May; four men and one woman killed and eight or ten beaten in June; most others ordered to leave. Names 'could not be learned'.
A Black man (or family) accused of jumping a crop after receiving advances from the Bruce brothers; Black men accused of ambushing and shooting Craft and, later, Boyles
The Bruce brothers and neighbors (May posse); June killings attributed to men from southern Smith County, 'the noted Sullivan's Hollow community', Craft's section
'Several' in May (unverified, secondhand); four men and one woman in June
Reported quiet by June 8-9, conditional on the Black residents ordered out leaving 'at once'
